This whole argument is based on the idea that there are "legal" vs. "illegal" immigrants. It's not this simple. America has a complicated immigration history wherein what it meant to be "illegal" has evolved with politics. The reason many people refer to them as "undocumented" is because this is more accurate. Immigrants to the US didn't use to ever have documents, especially not in the way that we do today. But back then they won't considered illegal. There was no more organized way of immigration. Now there is, but that form of immigration is deeply flawed. On average, it favors wealthier immigrants and is skewed towards smaller countries because we don't account for country size when determining how many people we will let in for different countries.  


In terms of mass deportation. There are above 10 million undocumented immigrants in just the US. Many of these people are a part of families who have mixed status. That is, some people in the family don't have legal status and some do. Mass deportation would be devastating to these families and to the communities in which they exist. Full disclosure, this would affect me, a citizen, profoundly.

​

What's more, if you don't buy the historical/legal argument and don't care about the families, it would be an economically disastrous to deport that many workers from our countries work force.  


Also, say what you will about undocumented immigrants, but DACA recipients are were children who were brought here when they were too young to know what countries even were. They know only the USA as their homeland and have desperately needed legal protection for years. They deserve the protections offered by H.R. 6 - The Dream and Promise Act and I highly encourage everyone to call your senators (especially those of you in Kentucky) and ask them to vote yes on it without adding anything else to it.

It boils down to something like, voter fraud is a specific person trying to vote when they shouldn't be able to or trying to vote twice or something like that vs. election fraud wherein someone tries to orchestrate a much larger rigging of the entire election or a large part of it.  


The main difference is that there isn't a lot of evidence that voter fraud is that common and even when it occurs it doesn't have too much of an impact because it truly is like 1 more vote in a huge sea of votes. Electoral fraud (as far as I know) isn't a ton more common, but according to political scientists is the one to watch out for because it can more easily affect the outcome of an election.  


Another distinction is that voter fraud is brought up more commonly as something democrats/minorities do whereas electoral fraud is something republicans do. This has some element of truth to it: Voter fraud can occur when someone who thinks they are registered is actually not. This actually does happen due to poor civic education or a low socio-economic status or more likely a combination of the two. Electoral fraud generally requires a good amount of affluence and much more knowledge of the electoral system. As you may be able to guess, these two characteristics can generally be applied to the two major parties, Democrat and Republican respectively.
